README.md — WeIntern Task 3

WeIntern Internship — Task 3

Deploy a Static Website Using Amazon S3 and Amazon CloudFront

Author: Swapna Adhav
Project: WeIntern Internship
Task: Task 3 — Deploy a Static Site via S3 / GCS
Cloud Provider: Amazon Web Services (AWS)
Region: Asia Pacific (Sydney) — ap-southeast-2
Status: Successfully deployed and verified

1. Project Overview

The objective of this project is to deploy a static website using Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and Amazon CloudFront.

The HTML website is stored in an S3 bucket. CloudFront distributes the website to visitors over HTTPS. The S3 bucket remains private, and CloudFront uses Origin Access Control (OAC) to access the website files.

Live Website

Website URL: https://dwpuiw40xj1jx.cloudfront.net/

GitHub Repository: https://github.com/adhavswapna/Weintern-Internship

2. Objectives

  • Create an Amazon S3 bucket.

  • Configure the AWS region and resource tags.

  • Keep the S3 bucket private by blocking public access.

  • Upload the static website's index.html file.

  • Configure CloudFront to distribute the website.

  • Use Origin Access Control (OAC) to protect the S3 origin.

  • Configure a bucket policy to allow CloudFront to read website files.

  • Redirect HTTP requests to HTTPS.

  • Verify the deployment and document the results.

3. Technologies Used

  • Amazon S3: Stores the static website files.

  • Amazon CloudFront: Distributes the website to visitors.

  • Origin Access Control (OAC): Allows CloudFront to access the private S3 origin.

  • AWS CLI: Creates and manages AWS resources from the terminal.

  • HTML and CSS: Build and style the website.

  • Git and GitHub: Version control and project documentation.

  • Python 3: Basic HTML and JSON validation.

How It Works

  1. A visitor opens the CloudFront website URL.

  2. CloudFront receives the HTTPS request.

  3. CloudFront retrieves the requested file from the S3 bucket using OAC.

  4. The S3 bucket policy authorizes read access for the specified CloudFront distribution.

  5. CloudFront returns the website content to the visitor.

The S3 bucket is not configured for public access.

6. Prerequisites

Before starting, ensure you have:

  • An AWS account.

  • AWS CLI installed.

  • AWS CLI configured with suitable permissions.

  • Python 3 installed.

  • A GitHub account.

  • A local project directory containing index.html.

Verify your AWS CLI installation:

aws --version

Check the active AWS identity:

aws sts get-caller-identity

Check the configured AWS region:

aws configure get region

The configured region for this project is:

ap-southeast-2

7. Step-by-Step Implementation

Step 1: Configure Environment Variables

Set the variables used by the AWS CLI commands.

export AWS_REGION="ap-southeast-2"
export BUCKET_NAME="weintern-task3-s3-swapnaadhav"
export PROJECT="WeIntern-Internship"
export TASK="Task3"
export ENVIRONMENT="Learning"
export OWNER="SwapnaAdhav"

Verify the variables:

echo "$AWS_REGION"
echo "$BUCKET_NAME"

Step 2: Create the S3 Bucket

Create the S3 bucket in the Sydney region.

aws s3api create-bucket \
  --bucket "$BUCKET_NAME" \
  --region "$AWS_REGION" \
  --create-bucket-configuration LocationConstraint="$AWS_REGION"

Result: The bucket weintern-task3-s3-swapnaadhav was created.

Step 3: Block Public Access

Configure all four S3 Block Public Access settings.

aws s3api put-public-access-block \
  --bucket "$BUCKET_NAME" \
  --region "$AWS_REGION" \
  --public-access-block-configuration \
  'BlockPublicAcls=true,IgnorePublicAcls=true,BlockPublicPolicy=true,RestrictPublicBuckets=true'

Verify the settings:

aws s3api get-public-access-block \
  --bucket "$BUCKET_NAME" \
  --region "$AWS_REGION"

Verified result: All four settings returned true.

This configuration helps prevent accidental public access to the bucket.

Step 4: Add Bucket Tags

Apply tags to identify the project and its owner.

aws s3api put-bucket-tagging \
  --bucket "$BUCKET_NAME" \
  --region "$AWS_REGION" \
  --tagging 'TagSet=[
    {Key=Project,Value=WeIntern-Internship},
    {Key=Task,Value=Task3},
    {Key=Environment,Value=Learning},
    {Key=Owner,Value=SwapnaAdhav}
  ]'

Verify the tags:

aws s3api get-bucket-tagging \
  --bucket "$BUCKET_NAME" \
  --region "$AWS_REGION"

Step 5: Upload the Website

Navigate to the project directory.

cd ~/weintern-cloud-internship/task3-static-website

Upload index.html to S3.

aws s3 cp index.html \
  "s3://$BUCKET_NAME/index.html" \
  --region "$AWS_REGION" \
  --content-type "text/html"

Verify the uploaded object:

aws s3api head-object \
  --bucket "$BUCKET_NAME" \
  --key index.html \
  --region "$AWS_REGION"

Verified results:

  • Content type: text/html

  • Server-side encryption: AES256

  • Object key: index.html

Step 6: Configure CloudFront Origin Access Control

An Origin Access Control was created to let CloudFront access the private S3 origin.

OAC ID: E2M1DLNO7XA6O4

The S3 origin used by the distribution is:

weintern-task3-s3-swapnaadhav.s3.ap-southeast-2.amazonaws.com

OAC provides authenticated origin access without making the bucket public.

Step 7: Create the CloudFront Distribution

The CloudFront distribution was configured with the following settings:

  • Default root object: index.html

  • Viewer protocol policy: redirect-to-https

  • Allowed methods: GET and HEAD

  • Compression: enabled

  • Price class: PriceClass_100

  • CloudFront default certificate: enabled

  • HTTP/2: enabled

  • IPv6: enabled

  • Origin: the S3 bucket's REST endpoint

  • Origin access: OAC

The distribution was created successfully.

Distribution ID:

EAGMUDC8KCZVQ

Distribution ARN:

arn:aws:cloudfront::230623977579:distribution/EAGMUDC8KCZVQ

CloudFront Domain:

dwpuiw40xj1jx.cloudfront.net

Step 8: Configure the S3 Bucket Policy

The bucket policy allows CloudFront to read objects from the bucket.

The policy uses the CloudFront service principal and restricts access to the specific distribution ARN.

The key permissions are:

  • Principal: cloudfront.amazonaws.com

  • Action: s3:GetObject

  • Resource: arn:aws:s3:::weintern-task3-s3-swapnaadhav/*

  • Condition: the request must originate from the specified CloudFront distribution.

Validate the JSON file:

python3 -m json.tool bucket-policy.json

Security note: Keep all four S3 Block Public Access settings enabled. Do not make the bucket public as a workaround for access errors.

Step 9: Verify CloudFront Deployment

Check the distribution status:

aws cloudfront get-distribution \
  --id EAGMUDC8KCZVQ \
  --query 'Distribution.Status' \
  --output text

Verified result:

Deployed

Step 10: Upload Website Updates

Whenever you modify index.html, upload it again:

aws s3 cp index.html \
  s3://weintern-task3-s3-swapnaadhav/index.html \
  --region ap-southeast-2 \
  --content-type "text/html"

Step 11: Invalidate the CloudFront Cache

Request an invalidation so CloudFront refreshes cached website content.

aws cloudfront create-invalidation \
  --distribution-id EAGMUDC8KCZVQ \
  --paths "/*"

The recorded invalidation requests initially returned InProgress.

To check the final status, use the invalidation ID returned by the command:

aws cloudfront get-invalidation \
  --distribution-id EAGMUDC8KCZVQ \
  --id YOUR_INVALIDATION_ID \
  --query 'Invalidation.Status' \
  --output text

Replace YOUR_INVALIDATION_ID with the actual ID.

Step 12: Verify the Website URL

Retrieve the CloudFront domain:

aws cloudfront get-distribution \
  --id EAGMUDC8KCZVQ \
  --query 'Distribution.DomainName' \
  --output text

Check the website response:

curl -I https://dwpuiw40xj1jx.cloudfront.net/

Verified result: The endpoint returned HTTP/2 200.

Open the website:

https://dwpuiw40xj1jx.cloudfront.net/

Step 13: Validate the HTML File

A basic HTML parser check can be performed using Python:

python3 - <<'PY'
from html.parser import HTMLParser
from pathlib import Path

class Validator(HTMLParser):
    pass

html = Path("index.html").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
Validator().feed(html)
print("HTML parser completed without a syntax error.")
PY

This checks whether Python's HTML parser can process the file. It is not a complete accessibility or browser-compatibility test.

9. GitHub Repository Setup

cd ~/weintern-cloud-internship/task3-static-website

Check Git status:

If no origin remote exists, add it:

git push -u origin main

GitHub Authentication

GitHub does not accept a normal account password for HTTPS Git operations.

Use one of these methods:

  • Git Credential Manager or browser authentication.

  • A fine-grained Personal Access Token with access to the correct repository and Contents: Read and write.

  • SSH authentication using an SSH key registered with GitHub.

Never share your token or commit it to the repository.

If GitHub rejects the push because the remote already contains commits, inspect the repository history and reconcile it before pushing. Do not force-push automatically.

10. Security Considerations

  • S3 Block Public Access remains enabled.

  • CloudFront accesses the origin through OAC.

  • The bucket policy restricts object reads to the intended distribution.

  • Viewer requests are redirected to HTTPS.

  • The uploaded object was observed to use AES256 server-side encryption.

  • AWS credentials and GitHub tokens must never be committed.

  • Consider enabling S3 versioning if recovery of older files is required.

  • Review AWS costs before leaving cloud resources running.

11. Troubleshooting

Error: 403 Forbidden

Check that:

  • CloudFront is deployed.

  • OAC is attached to the correct S3 origin.

  • The bucket policy contains the correct distribution ARN.

  • index.html exists in S3.

  • The CloudFront distribution is configured for the correct origin.

Do not make the bucket public to resolve this error.

Error: 404 Not Found

Check that:

  • The uploaded object key is index.html.

  • The default root object is index.html.

  • The CloudFront origin points to the correct bucket.

Website Updates Are Not Visible

Upload the updated file, create a CloudFront invalidation, and wait for it to complete.

GitHub Authentication Failed

Do not use the normal GitHub account password. Check the token's expiration, repository access, and Contents: Read and write permission.

12. Optional Cleanup

Warning: The following commands delete the S3 website files and bucket. Only run them if you no longer need the deployment.

aws s3 rm s3://weintern-task3-s3-swapnaadhav \
  --recursive \
  --region ap-southeast-2

Then delete the bucket:

aws s3api delete-bucket \
  --bucket weintern-task3-s3-swapnaadhav \
  --region ap-southeast-2

CloudFront must be disabled and the configuration update fully deployed before the distribution can be deleted. Follow the current AWS CLI procedure for CloudFront deletion.

13. Conclusion

The static website was uploaded to Amazon S3 and distributed through Amazon CloudFront over HTTPS.

S3 public access blocking remained enabled, and CloudFront OAC together with a scoped bucket policy provided controlled access to the private S3 origin.

The CloudFront distribution reached Deployed status, and the live HTTPS endpoint returned HTTP/2 200.

WeIntern Task 3 — Formal Project Report

WEINTERN INTERNSHIP

Task 3: Deploy a Static Website Using Amazon S3 and Amazon CloudFront

Prepared by: Swapna Adhav
Cloud Provider: Amazon Web Services (AWS)
AWS Region: Asia Pacific (Sydney) — ap-southeast-2

1. Introduction

The purpose of this internship task was to deploy a static website using cloud infrastructure. Amazon S3 was used to store the HTML website files, while Amazon CloudFront was used to distribute the website securely over HTTPS.

The project demonstrates cloud storage, content delivery, access control, AWS CLI usage, and deployment verification.

The S3 bucket was configured to block public access. CloudFront accesses the bucket using Origin Access Control (OAC), and the bucket policy limits object-read access to the intended CloudFront distribution.

2. Project Objectives

The main objectives were:

  1. Create an S3 bucket in the Sydney AWS region.

  2. Configure S3 Block Public Access.

  3. Add project tags to the bucket.

  4. Upload the static website's index.html file.

  5. Create and configure a CloudFront distribution.

  6. Configure Origin Access Control.

  7. Apply a bucket policy that permits the CloudFront distribution to read website objects.

  8. Redirect HTTP requests to HTTPS.

  9. Validate the deployment and confirm that the website is accessible.

  10. Document the implementation for GitHub.

3. Tools and Services

Amazon S3

Amazon S3 stores the static HTML file used by the website.

Amazon CloudFront

CloudFront delivers the website content to visitors and supports HTTPS access.

Origin Access Control

OAC allows CloudFront to make authenticated requests to the private S3 origin.

AWS CLI

The AWS Command Line Interface was used to create, configure, inspect, and verify cloud resources.

HTML, CSS, Git, and GitHub

HTML and CSS were used for the website. Git and GitHub were used for version control and documentation.

4. Project Architecture

The deployment uses the following architecture:

User Browser
     |
     | HTTPS request
     v
Amazon CloudFront
     |
     | Authenticated origin request through OAC
     v
Private Amazon S3 Bucket
     |
     v
index.html

Architecture Explanation

A visitor opens the CloudFront URL in a browser. CloudFront receives the request and retrieves the website object from the S3 origin through OAC.

The S3 bucket policy authorizes object reads from the specified CloudFront distribution. Public access blocking remains enabled on the bucket.

This design separates public website delivery from direct public access to the storage bucket.

6. Implementation Procedure

Step 1: Verify AWS CLI Configuration

The AWS identity and region were checked before deploying resources.

aws sts get-caller-identity
aws configure get region

The configured region was:

ap-southeast-2

The caller identity command returned an IAM user identity for the AWS account used in this project.

Step 2: Define Environment Variables

The following variables were set in the terminal:

export AWS_REGION="ap-southeast-2"
export BUCKET_NAME="weintern-task3-s3-swapnaadhav"
export PROJECT="WeIntern-Internship"
export TASK="Task3"
export ENVIRONMENT="Learning"
export OWNER="SwapnaAdhav"

These variables simplify the commands by avoiding repeated entry of resource names.

Step 3: Create the S3 Bucket

The bucket was created in the Sydney region using:

aws s3api create-bucket \
  --bucket "$BUCKET_NAME" \
  --region "$AWS_REGION" \
  --create-bucket-configuration LocationConstraint="$AWS_REGION"

The resulting bucket name was:

weintern-task3-s3-swapnaadhav

Step 4: Configure Block Public Access

All four S3 Block Public Access settings were enabled:

aws s3api put-public-access-block \
  --bucket "$BUCKET_NAME" \
  --region "$AWS_REGION" \
  --public-access-block-configuration \
  'BlockPublicAcls=true,IgnorePublicAcls=true,BlockPublicPolicy=true,RestrictPublicBuckets=true'

The configuration was verified with:

aws s3api get-public-access-block \
  --bucket "$BUCKET_NAME" \
  --region "$AWS_REGION"

Result: All four settings were returned as true.

This reduces the risk of accidentally exposing the bucket directly to the public.

Step 5: Apply Bucket Tags

The bucket was tagged for project identification and organization.

aws s3api put-bucket-tagging \
  --bucket "$BUCKET_NAME" \
  --region "$AWS_REGION" \
  --tagging 'TagSet=[
    {Key=Project,Value=WeIntern-Internship},
    {Key=Task,Value=Task3},
    {Key=Environment,Value=Learning},
    {Key=Owner,Value=SwapnaAdhav}
  ]'

The tags were checked with:

aws s3api get-bucket-tagging \
  --bucket "$BUCKET_NAME" \
  --region "$AWS_REGION"

The bucket tags identify the project, task, environment, and owner.

Step 6: Upload the Website File

The website file was uploaded to S3 with the correct content type.

aws s3 cp index.html \
  "s3://$BUCKET_NAME/index.html" \
  --region "$AWS_REGION" \
  --content-type "text/html"

The uploaded object was inspected using:

aws s3api head-object \
  --bucket "$BUCKET_NAME" \
  --key index.html \
  --region "$AWS_REGION"

Observed results:

  • Object key: index.html

  • Content type: text/html

  • Server-side encryption: AES256

Step 7: Configure Origin Access Control

An Origin Access Control was created for CloudFront.

OAC ID: E2M1DLNO7XA6O4

OAC enables CloudFront to make authenticated requests to the private S3 origin. This allows the website to be delivered through CloudFront without making the bucket publicly accessible.

Step 8: Create the CloudFront Distribution

The CloudFront distribution was configured to use the S3 REST endpoint as its origin.

The configuration included:

  • index.html as the default root object.

  • Redirecting HTTP requests to HTTPS.

  • Allowing GET and HEAD requests.

  • Enabling response compression.

  • Using the CloudFront default certificate.

  • Selecting PriceClass_100.

  • Enabling HTTP/2 and IPv6.

  • Associating the OAC with the S3 origin.

The distribution was created successfully.

Distribution ID:

EAGMUDC8KCZVQ

Distribution ARN:

arn:aws:cloudfront::230623977579:distribution/EAGMUDC8KCZVQ

CloudFront Domain:

dwpuiw40xj1jx.cloudfront.net

Step 9: Configure the Bucket Policy

The bucket policy permits the CloudFront service principal to read website objects. It restricts the permission to the intended CloudFront distribution ARN.

The main policy components are:

  • Principal: cloudfront.amazonaws.com

  • Action: s3:GetObject

  • Resource: objects inside the project bucket

  • Condition: the request's source ARN must match the CloudFront distribution ARN.

The JSON policy file was validated using:

python3 -m json.tool bucket-policy.json

The policy provides read-only object access rather than unrestricted S3 access.

Deployed

This confirms that CloudFront reported the distribution as deployed at the time of verification.

After uploading an updated HTML file, a CloudFront invalidation was requested.

aws cloudfront create-invalidation \

  --paths "/*"

The recorded invalidation requests initially returned InProgress.

The invalidation status can be checked using the ID returned by the command:

aws cloudfront get-invalidation \

  --query 'Invalidation.Status' \

The invalidation should be confirmed as Completed before reporting it as fully finished.

aws cloudfront get-distribution \

curl -I https://dwpuiw40xj1jx.cloudfront.net/

8. Security Measures

The following security measures were used:

  1. Block Public Access: All four S3 Block Public Access settings were enabled.

  2. Private S3 Origin: The bucket was not made publicly readable.

  3. Origin Access Control: CloudFront used OAC to access the S3 origin.

  4. Scoped Bucket Policy: Read permission was restricted to the intended CloudFront distribution.

  5. HTTPS Redirection: Viewer requests were configured to redirect from HTTP to HTTPS.

  6. Server-Side Encryption: The uploaded object was observed to use AES256 server-side encryption.

  7. Credential Protection: AWS credentials and GitHub tokens must remain outside the source repository.

10. Troubleshooting

10.1 Access Denied or 403 Error

Check that:

  • The CloudFront distribution is deployed.

  • OAC is attached to the correct origin.

  • The bucket policy references the correct distribution ARN.

  • The index.html object exists.

  • The distribution uses the correct S3 origin.

Do not make the bucket public to resolve this error.

10.2 404 Error

Check the object key and verify that CloudFront uses index.html as its default root object.

10.3 Website Changes Are Not Visible

Upload the updated file, create a CloudFront invalidation, and wait for it to complete.

10.4 GitHub Authentication Failure

Use a valid token or another supported authentication method. Confirm the token has access to the correct repository and that the required repository permissions are enabled.

Never include the token in project documentation or source files.

CloudFront must be disabled and the configuration change deployed before deleting the distribution. Follow the current AWS CLI deletion procedure and verify all related resources before cleanup.

12. Conclusion

This project successfully deployed a static website using Amazon S3 and Amazon CloudFront.

The website files were stored in S3, and CloudFront distributed the content over HTTPS. The S3 bucket's public access blocking remained enabled, while OAC and a scoped bucket policy controlled access to the private origin.

WEINTERN INTERNSHIP
Task 3: Deploy a Static Website Using Amazon S3 and Amazon CloudFront

Prepared by Swapna Adhav | AWS Region: ap-southeast-2

1. Introduction

This project deploys a static HTML website using Amazon S3 and Amazon CloudFront. S3 stores the website file, while CloudFront distributes the content over HTTPS. The S3 bucket remains private, and CloudFront uses Origin Access Control (OAC) to access the origin.

Live website: https://dwpuiw40xj1jx.cloudfront.net/

GitHub repository: https://github.com/adhavswapna/Weintern-Internship

2. Project Objectives

Create an S3 bucket in the Sydney AWS region.

Enable all four S3 Block Public Access settings.

Tag the bucket and upload index.html.

Configure CloudFront with HTTPS redirection and index.html as the default root object.

Use OAC and a scoped bucket policy to permit CloudFront to read objects.

Validate the deployed website and document the results.

3. Tools and Services

Amazon S3 — storage for the static HTML website.

Amazon CloudFront — content delivery and HTTPS access.

Origin Access Control — authenticated access from CloudFront to the private S3 origin.

AWS CLI — resource creation and verification.

HTML/CSS — website content and styling.

Git/GitHub — version control and project documentation.

Python 3 — basic HTML and JSON validation.

4. Architecture

Visitor Browser --HTTPS--> Amazon CloudFront --OAC-authenticated request--> Private S3 bucket (index.html)

A visitor opens the CloudFront URL. CloudFront retrieves the file from S3 through OAC. The bucket policy restricts s3:GetObject access to the specified CloudFront distribution. S3 Block Public Access remains enabled.

6. Step-by-Step Implementation

Step 1 — Verify AWS CLI configuration

aws --version
aws sts get-caller-identity
aws configure get region

The configured region was ap-southeast-2. The caller identity command returned the IAM identity used for this deployment.

Step 2 — Set environment variables

export AWS_REGION="ap-southeast-2"
export BUCKET_NAME="weintern-task3-s3-swapnaadhav"
export PROJECT="WeIntern-Internship"
export TASK="Task3"
export ENVIRONMENT="Learning"
export OWNER="SwapnaAdhav"

Step 3 — Create the S3 bucket

aws s3api create-bucket \
--bucket "$BUCKET_NAME" \
--region "$AWS_REGION" \
--create-bucket-configuration LocationConstraint="$AWS_REGION"

The bucket was created in the Sydney region.

Step 4 — Block public access

aws s3api put-public-access-block \
--bucket "$BUCKET_NAME" \
--region "$AWS_REGION" \
--public-access-block-configuration \
'BlockPublicAcls=true,IgnorePublicAcls=true,BlockPublicPolicy=true,RestrictPublicBuckets=true'

aws s3api get-public-access-block --bucket "$BUCKET_NAME" --region "$AWS_REGION"

Verification showed all four Block Public Access settings set to true.

Step 5 — Tag the bucket

aws s3api put-bucket-tagging \
--bucket "$BUCKET_NAME" --region "$AWS_REGION" \
--tagging 'TagSet=[{Key=Project,Value=WeIntern-Internship},{Key=Task,Value=Task3},{Key=Environment,Value=Learning},{Key=Owner,Value=SwapnaAdhav}]'

aws s3api get-bucket-tagging --bucket "$BUCKET_NAME" --region "$AWS_REGION"

Tags identify the project, task, learning environment, and owner.

Step 6 — Upload index.html

cd ~/weintern-cloud-internship/task3-static-website
aws s3 cp index.html "s3://$BUCKET_NAME/index.html" --region "$AWS_REGION" --content-type "text/html"

aws s3api head-object --bucket "$BUCKET_NAME" --key index.html --region "$AWS_REGION"

The uploaded object was verified with content type text/html and AES256 server-side encryption.

Step 7 — Configure CloudFront and OAC

An Origin Access Control was created with ID E2M1DLNO7XA6O4. The CloudFront distribution uses the S3 REST origin weintern-task3-s3-swapnaadhav.s3.ap-southeast-2.amazonaws.com.

The distribution configuration includes index.html as the default root object, redirect-to-https, GET/HEAD methods, compression, PriceClass_100, the CloudFront default certificate, HTTP/2, and IPv6.

The distribution ID is EAGMUDC8KCZVQ, its ARN is arn:aws:cloudfront::230623977579:distribution/EAGMUDC8KCZVQ, and its domain is dwpuiw40xj1jx.cloudfront.net.

Configuration note: the draft configuration pasted into the terminal contained placeholder origin text and a nonstandard IPv6 property. Use the live distribution configuration as authoritative rather than reusing that draft unchanged.

Step 8 — Apply and validate the bucket policy

The bucket policy grants the CloudFront service principal s3:GetObject on the bucket's objects, with AWS:SourceArn restricted to the CloudFront distribution ARN.

python3 -m json.tool bucket-policy.json

This is read-only object access scoped to the intended distribution.

Step 9 — Verify CloudFront deployment

aws cloudfront get-distribution --id EAGMUDC8KCZVQ --query 'Distribution.Status' --output text

Observed result: Deployed.

Step 10 — Invalidate the cache after updates

aws cloudfront create-invalidation --distribution-id EAGMUDC8KCZVQ --paths "/*"

The recorded invalidation requests initially returned InProgress. Check the final status using the invalidation ID returned by the command:

aws cloudfront get-invalidation --distribution-id EAGMUDC8KCZVQ --id YOUR_INVALIDATION_ID --query 'Invalidation.Status' --output text

Step 11 — Verify the website

aws cloudfront get-distribution --id EAGMUDC8KCZVQ --query 'Distribution.DomainName' --output text
curl -I https://dwpuiw40xj1jx.cloudfront.net/

Observed result: the HTTPS endpoint returned HTTP/2 200.

8. GitHub Publishing

The intended repository is https://github.com/adhavswapna/Weintern-Internship.

cd ~/weintern-cloud-internship/task3-static-website
git status
git remote -v

If the origin remote is missing, add it; if it points to a different repository, update it:

git remote set-url origin https://github.com/adhavswapna/Weintern-Internship.git

Stage and commit the intended files, then push:

git add index.html README.md .gitignore
git commit -m "Document AWS static website deployment"
git push -u origin main

GitHub does not accept normal account passwords for HTTPS Git operations. Use Git Credential Manager/browser authentication, a fine-grained PAT with access to the repository and Contents: Read and write, or SSH. Never share or commit tokens. If the remote has existing commits, reconcile histories rather than force-pushing.

9. Security Considerations

All four S3 Block Public Access settings remain enabled.

CloudFront accesses the private S3 origin using OAC.

The bucket policy scopes object reads to the intended distribution.

Viewer requests are redirected to HTTPS.

The uploaded object was observed to use AES256 server-side encryption.

AWS credentials and GitHub tokens must not be committed to Git.

10. Troubleshooting

403 Forbidden

Check the CloudFront deployment status, OAC attachment, bucket policy SourceArn, S3 object key, and origin. Do not make the bucket public as a workaround.

404 Not Found

Confirm that index.html exists and is configured as the CloudFront default root object.

Website changes do not appear

Upload the new HTML file, create an invalidation, and wait for it to complete.

GitHub authentication failed

Do not use the GitHub account password. Check PAT expiration, repository access, and Contents: Read and write permission. Never share the token.

11. Optional Cleanup

Only run these commands if the website is no longer needed. They delete the website objects and bucket:

aws s3 rm s3://weintern-task3-s3-swapnaadhav --recursive --region ap-southeast-2
aws s3api delete-bucket --bucket weintern-task3-s3-swapnaadhav --region ap-southeast-2

CloudFront must be disabled and its configuration update deployed before deleting the distribution. Follow the current AWS CLI procedure and review all project resources before cleanup.

12. Conclusion

The static website was uploaded to Amazon S3 and distributed through Amazon CloudFront over HTTPS. S3 public access blocking remained enabled, while OAC and a scoped bucket policy controlled access to the private origin. The distribution reached Deployed status, and the live HTTPS endpoint returned HTTP/2 200.

Live website: https://dwpuiw40xj1jx.cloudfront.net/
